blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
Iterative fine-tuning on synthetic data causes model collapse : output
diversity narrows as rare patterns are progressively lost, a signature most
visible as phrase-level repetition. Existing
mitigations either require model log-probabilities, an external oracle, or continued
access to real human data. Here we develop a new approach grounded in mathematical information theory: the non-parametric Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , computed entirely from raw text via match-length statistics, with no
model of any kind. We show that this is in fact a superior training-data filter on text-diversity
metrics in a fully-synthetic, single-lineage fine-tuning setting.
In a six-generation QLoRA collapse experiment on
Llama-3.1-8B, logprob-based filtering (the most established model-access-requiring baseline) provides
no significant text-diversity benefit on any metric ( p > 0.23 p>0.23 ), whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering yields + 42 % +42\% unique trigrams, + 30 % +30\% vocabulary, and − 19 % -19\% repetition (all p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). We validate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a cross-domain
entropy proxy ( β = 0.924 \beta=0.924 , R 2 = 0.746 R^{2}=0.746 ) and collapse detector
( ρ = + 0.454 \rho=+0.454 , p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ) across 4 domains, 2 temperatures,
2 generator–scorer model pairs, and 1,520 generated documents.
Our results demonstrate that information theoretic approaches to collapse mitigation are efficient, and suggest new approaches for maintaining multi-agent diversity.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Large language models trained on their own outputs face a self-reinforcing
degradation known as model collapse : when a model’s outputs are
used to fine-tune successor models, the entropy of the output distribution
declines across generations, diversity narrows, and rare linguistic patterns
are progressively lost ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ) . As synthetic content becomes an increasing fraction of web-scraped training
corpora, collapse mitigation is shifting from a theoretical concern to an
engineering requirement for production training pipelines.

blocks.en:
Existing mitigations for model collapse fall into one of three categories:
(A) model
logprob filters such as surplexity filtering ( Gambetta et al., 2026 ) ,
which scores documents by the model’s own per-token Shannon entropy and retains
those the model finds surprising;
(B) external oracle or classifier
approaches utilising an independent language model; and
(C) data accumulation strategies that re-inject real human data
at each generation ( Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Bertrand et al., 2024 ) .
Among filtering approaches that do not require the injection of real, expensive human data, surplexity filtering is the most established model-access-requiring baseline. Gambetta et al. (2026) demonstrate that it delays collapse as measured
by the model’s own entropy and perplexity scores, but its effect on
independent text-diversity measures has not been evaluated. Throughout this
paper we compare against mean per-token Shannon entropy H L H_{L} specifically,
which is closely related to but not necessarily identical to surplexity:
both are monotonically increasing functions of the model’s output entropy,
but surplexity uses the sample surprise of the generated tokens whereas H L H_{L} averages over the full output distribution, so the two induce highly
similar but not necessarily identical document rankings. Moreover, Guo et al. (2024) find that linguistic acceptability filtering can
actually worsen collapse, underscoring that the choice of filtering
criterion is consequential.

blocks.en:
Surplexity filtering requires a forward pass through the model being trained,
with access to the full next-token distribution at each position. Such access
is unavailable for closed-source APIs, computationally expensive at scale, and
version-dependent – the same document receives different surplexity scores as
the model is updated. Data accumulation avoids model access but presupposes a
continuing supply of human-authored text, which is costly and slow to generate, and unavailable in a fully
synthetic closed loop. A text-only collapse filter that requires no model of
any kind would be strictly preferable, even if it were found to be less effective than surplexity filtering.

blocks.en:
Motivated by results from mathematical information theory, we propose the Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ( Kontoyiannis et al., 1998 ) as a text-only collapse filter and show that it
outperforms logprob-based filtering. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} estimates the entropy rate of a
symbolic sequence by measuring match lengths: at each position, it records the
length of the longest prefix of the remaining text that has previously appeared
in the document. Long matches signal repetition in the text; short matches signal
novelty. The Kontoyiannis estimator has previously been used to quantify information flow in social
media text ( Bagrow et al., 2019 ; Bagrow and Mitchell, 2018 ; Pond et al., 2020 ) and requires no
model, no API, and no GPU. To our knowledge, no prior work has applied H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} or any compression-rate statistic as a collapse filter; it is the only
proposed filter of this type requiring no model of any kind – not a forward
pass, not an oracle, not a reference classifier.

blocks.en: 2 Background and Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 背景和有关工作

blocks.en:
Shumailov et al. (2024) demonstrate that iterative training on model-generated
data causes progressive loss of distributional tails: output variance shrinks
across generations as the model reinforces its existing biases. The phenomenon
is formalised by Alemohammad et al. (2024) , who show that without real-data
anchoring, iterative self-distillation inevitably converges to low-entropy
output. Briesch et al. (2023) provide the first LLM-specific empirical study of
self-consuming training loops, finding that diversity declines in proportion to
the synthetic data fraction. Measuring collapse in terms of text-level diversity is a more recent development: Guo et al. (2024) conduct
iterative fine-tuning on NLG tasks and track lexical, syntactic, and semantic
diversity across generations, observing that syntactic diversity deteriorates
fastest and creative tasks are most vulnerable. Both works characterise
collapse through output distribution statistics; we measure it directly via the
entropy rate of the generated text. Analogous diversity collapse has been
documented in multi-agent LLM systems, where structural coupling during
iterative interaction drives premature semantic convergence even without any
weight update ( Chen et al., 2026 ) ; the present work identifies a
complementary mechanism operating through the fine-tuning data loop.

Existing mitigations fall into three broad categories, each imposing a
distinct requirement on the practitioner.

(A) Model-logprob methods. Gambetta et al. (2026) propose surplexity – the product of token-level
surprise and perplexity – as a data-quality signal for collapse mitigation.
In practice, retaining high-surplexity documents is closely related to
filtering by the mean Shannon entropy of the generator’s next-token
distribution, which we denote H L H_{L} . This is the text-level analogue of
perplexity-based data filtering widely used in large-scale pretraining
pipelines ( Wenzek et al., 2020 ) . Zhu et al. (2025) resample tokens
whose predicted probability exceeds a threshold from a prior language model,
requiring token-level logprobs during generation, while Alemohammad et al. (2024) show that biased or top- K K sampling – retaining only
the highest-scoring synthetic samples each generation – can slow collapse when
a quality score derived from model internals is available. All three methods
require access to the generating model’s output distribution.

long-run convergence is toward the verifier’s biased knowledge centre,
not the true data distribution, unless the verifier is perfect. This finding
motivates the search for estimators that introduce no external model bias.

Each type of mitigation thus requires either model internals (A), a stronger external
model (B), or curated human data (C), imposing an extra burden to mitigate model collapse regardless of the approach taken.
In this work we introduce a novel filter in
category (D): H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is computed from raw text alone – no model, no API, no
GPU, no reference corpus – making it, to our knowledge, the only completely
model-free and reference-free model collapse filter proposed to date.

blocks.en:
Min-hash near-deduplication ( Lee et al., 2022 ; Penedo et al., 2024 ) is the standard model-free text-quality filter in large-scale pretraining
pipelines, and is the one existing method that, like H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering, requires
neither model access nor an external verifier. It removes near-duplicate documents from the training corpus (a between-document operation),
whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering selects documents by within-document phrase variety
(a within-document operation). The two approaches are complementary:
deduplication prevents the corpus from containing many copies of the same
text, while H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering ensures each document has not collapsed into
internally repetitive structure. A combined pipeline (deduplicate first,
then H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter) would address both failure modes.

process – no parametric assumptions on the token distribution are
required – where Λ i \Lambda_{i} is the length of the shortest prefix of x i , … , x n x_{i},\ldots,x_{n} that does not appear as a contiguous substring in x 1 , … , x i − 1 x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1} ; near the end of a document, where no such
non-appearing prefix may exist, Λ i \Lambda_{i} is bounded by the remaining
sequence length n − i n-i , so the sum in Equation ( 1 ) remains
well-defined without special-casing. Reported H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} values use the ProcessEntropy package’s tokenizer 2 2 2 https://github.com/tobinsouth/ProcessEntropy :
an NLTK TweetTokenizer pass, lower-cased, with non-alphanumeric characters
stripped from within each token ( South et al., 2022 ) . Real-time filtering decisions during
fine-tuning (Section 5 ) instead use a faster whitespace
tokenization (lower-case; non-alphanumeric characters replaced with
whitespace) for computational efficiency; the two agree closely in
practice (Spearman ρ = 0.997 \rho=0.997 on a held-out sample), so the choice
does not affect which documents are selected.
The estimator’s consistency is grounded in the Shannon–McMillan–Breiman
theorem ( Cover and Thomas, 2006 ) : for a stationary ergodic source, − 1 n ​ log 2 ⁡ P ⁡ ( X 1 , … , X n ) → H -\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}P(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\to H almost surely, and Λ i \Lambda_{i} serves as a nonparametric proxy for local self-information at
position i i – long matches signal low surprise; short matches signal high
surprise.
The match lengths also connect H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} to Lempel–Ziv (LZ) data
compression ( Ziv and Lempel, 1977 ; Ziv and Lempel, 1978 ) : each Λ i \Lambda_{i} identifies the shortest phrase at position i i not resolvable from prior
context – the elementary step of LZ parsing – so H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is interpretable
as a normalised LZ compression rate. While compression-based statistics have
been used for general data quality assessment, to our knowledge no prior work
has applied H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} or any LZ-derived metric as a model collapse mitigation filter.
At finite n n , H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is upward-biased: early positions have little past
context, so Λ i \Lambda_{i} is artificially small and the denominator is
deflated.
We control for this by computing H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} on the first 1,500 word tokens of
each document and discarding shorter texts (see Section 3 );
the residual finite-sample bias is reported as a limitation in
Section 6 .
The Kontoyiannis estimator provides a model-free measure of sequential complexity that
depends only on the text
itself ( Bagrow et al., 2019 ; Smart et al., 2024 ) .

blocks.en: Having established that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is a good collapse detector, we now consider our central question: can H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} be used to filter training data and mitigate collapse; and, if so, does it outperform H L H_{L} , the most established model-access-requiring baseline?
blocks.zh: 既然确定H^ K\hat{H}_{K}是一个很好的倒塌探测器,我们现在考虑我们的中心问题:H^ K\hat{H}_{K}能否被用来过滤训练数据并缓解倒塌;如果是的话,它是否超过了HL-H_{L},这是最固定的模型访问-要求基准?

distinction between H L H_{L} and surplexity proper); and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter : top 40 by Kontoyiannis entropy rate

blocks.en:
A natural objection is that any per-document diversity statistic might
replicate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s advantage – for instance, type–token ratio (TTR) or
bigram distinctiveness (Distinct-2). We assess this by simulating both
filters on the generation-0 pool, where all conditions share the same 80
documents and the comparison is exact. TTR@500-filtering selects training
documents with mean H ^ K = 3.37 \hat{H}_{K}=3.37 ; Distinct-2-filtering selects mean H ^ K = 3.32 \hat{H}_{K}=3.32 ; H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering selects mean H ^ K = 3.98 \hat{H}_{K}=3.98 – a 18–20%
advantage. Despite moderate positive correlations between TTR and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} in
the pool (Pearson r = 0.54 r=0.54 ), the selection sets overlap only 43% by
Jaccard, indicating that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} recovers phrase-level structure that
per-document surface statistics do not capture. The difference is structural:
TTR and Distinct-2 aggregate over short local windows, whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is
sensitive to long-range match structure – precisely the property that
fine-tuning collapse erodes.
We repeated this static-pool comparison against two further model-free
criteria: an off-the-shelf gzip-compression ratio (least-compressible 40
documents selected per domain) and an explicit 4-gram repetition-rate filter
(lowest repeated-4-gram rate). Both correlate with H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} only moderately
(gzip r = + 0.44 r=+0.44 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ; repetition rate r = − 0.36 r=-0.36 , p = 0.001 p=0.001 ) –
comparable to the TTR correlation above – and select substantially
different document sets (Jaccard 0.36 0.36 – 0.38 0.38 against the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter
selection). As with the TTR/Distinct-2 comparison, this establishes that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is related to but not redundant with either criterion on the static
pool, but not downstream collapse-resistance, which we test directly by
running both as genuine six-generation training filters, replacing H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} in
the filtering criterion but otherwise identical to Section 5 .
At generation 6, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering significantly outperforms both on every
metric ( H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , Distinct-3, Rep-4, vocabulary; all p < 0.005 p<0.005 , most p < 10 − 4 p<10^{-4} ). The two static-pool-comparable criteria do not perform alike
as real filters, however: gzip-filtering gives a modest but genuine
diversity benefit over unfiltered training (Distinct-3 + 17 % +17\% , vocabulary + 17 % +17\% , Rep-4 − 7 % -7\% ; all p < 0.03 p<0.03 ), while repetition-rate filtering gives
none (all four metrics indistinguishable from unfiltered, p > 0.24 p>0.24 ) despite
directly targeting repetition. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s advantage over simpler model-free
heuristics is therefore not just a static-pool artefact: it persists, and
in repetition-rate filtering’s case is entirely absent for the alternative,
under the same six-generation training loop that constitutes this paper’s
central result.

blocks.en:
We scored gen-6 documents from all conditions using
GPT-2 ( Radford et al., 2019 ) , a 124M-parameter model with no relation to
training or generation pipelines. GPT-2 entropy shows the same directional ordering ( H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtered > > H L H_{L} -filtered > > unfiltered) but does not reach significance ( p = 0.11 p=0.11 ),
limiting its value as independent validation; GPT-2’s discriminative power on
long-form text is insufficient to detect the effect at the individual-document
level. We also evaluated each generation’s fine-tuned checkpoint on
HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
(Figure 4 b). Accuracy drops sharply from
generation 0 to generation 1 ( 0.729 → ≈ 0.672 0.729\to\approx 0.672 ) and then plateaus
near 0.652 0.652 – 0.657 0.657 with no significant difference between conditions at any
generation. Thus H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering preserves text diversity but does not protect
general reasoning ability: the capability degradation introduced by iterative
fine-tuning is uniform across all three conditions. Two further downstream
benchmarks corroborate this: 5-shot MMLU and 8-shot GSM8K (1,000-example
subsamples each) on the same checkpoints show no significant difference
between conditions at generation 6 (MMLU: 67.6 67.6 – 67.6 % 67.6\% ; GSM8K: 70.7 70.7 – 71.2 % 71.2\% ; all pairwise χ 2 \chi^{2} tests p > 0.8 p>0.8 ), nor a significant
decline from generation 0 to generation 6 within any single condition
( p > 0.15 p>0.15 ) – consistent with HellaSwag, general capability retention is
unaffected by which text-diversity filter is used, at this scale and over
this many generations.

blocks.en: 6 Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论

blocks.en:
The Kontoyiannis estimator directly penalises repeated phrase structure: a
document with many recurring n n -grams exhibits long match lengths and hence a
low H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} . Fine-tuning collapse manifests primarily as increased phrase
repetition, so H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering targets collapse’s dominant surface signature
directly. H L H_{L} , by contrast, measures token-level uncertainty in the scorer
model – a signal that is destroyed after a single fine-tuning step, as shown
in Section 5 . At generation-0, H L H_{L} primarily
reflects topic familiarity – the wide bimodal distribution
documented in Figure 8 – rather than document diversity, so
a criterion uncorrelated with document quality at generation-0 cannot select
high-quality training data regardless of downstream variance. The result
suggests that collapse is fundamentally a phrase-repetition phenomenon, and
that phrase-level statistics are better positioned to detect it than
token-level uncertainty. A literal reimplementation of surplexity confirms
this mechanistic prediction directly: its median absolute deviation across
the shared generation-0 pool is 4.40 4.40 , falling to 0.40 0.40 – 0.49 0.49 (all three
conditions) after one fine-tuning step – a 9 9 – 11 11 -fold narrowing,
comparable to H L H_{L} ’s own collapse. (Generation-0 surplexity is heavy-tailed
– a handful of unfamiliar-topic documents receive extreme values once
surprise is exponentiated into perplexity – so median and MAD, not mean and
SD, are the meaningful summary here.)

Most importantly, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering preserves text diversity but does not protect
general reasoning ability: HellaSwag accuracy degrades equally across all three
filtering conditions (Figure 4 b), and MMLU and
GSM8K show the same pattern, so our claim is scoped to distributional
fidelity of generated text, not downstream task performance. The filtering
advantage is also specific to fine-tuning collapse:
under iterative rephrasing, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} tracks the aggregate trajectory but cannot
distinguish among documents within a generation, and is therefore unsuitable as
a within-generation filter in that setting. The diversity gains measured here are lexical: MAUVE scores ( Pillutla et al., 2021 ) (GPT-2-Large features, first 512 tokens) are near-ceiling and uniform across
conditions at generation 6 ( 0.987 0.987 – 0.993 0.993 ), indicating embedding-space
similarity is preserved and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s advantage is specific to within-document
match-length structure.
A separate concern is quality: selecting for match-length novelty could
favour incoherent or off-topic text over genuinely diverse text. We address
this directly with an LLM-judge pass (GPT-4o-mini, blind to condition)
scoring all 240 generation-6 documents (80 per condition) on two 1–5
scales, coherence and instruction-following, reading the full document so
that late-document degeneration is not missed. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering scores
highest of the three conditions on both:
coherence 2.35 2.35 versus 2.20 2.20 for unfiltered ( p = 0.058 p=0.058 ) and 2.29 2.29 for H L H_{L} -filtering; instruction-following 3.23 3.23 versus 3.00 3.00 for unfiltered
( p = 0.020 p=0.020 ) and 3.15 3.15 for H L H_{L} -filtering. If anything, then, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering’s diversity advantage comes with a small quality benefit
rather than a coherence cost. Finally, our collapse experiment uses a single model family (Llama-3.1, 8B);
replicating with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (same corpus and protocol), H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering
again retains more diversity at generation 6 ( 2.91 2.91 bits/word versus 2.12 2.12 unfiltered, p < 0.001 p<0.001 , and 2.41 2.41 for H L H_{L} -filtering, p = 0.004 p=0.004 ; H L H_{L} -filtering

different.

blocks.en:
The primary benefit is making collapse-resistant data curation accessible
without model access, reducing a practical barrier for organisations running
iterative fine-tuning under closed-source or resource-constrained conditions,
and counteracting homogenisation of AI-generated web content. The main negative
consequence is indirect: making fully-synthetic training pipelines more viable
may reduce the incentive to collect or compensate human-authored training data;
practitioners deploying such pipelines at scale should weigh this trade-off.

可能减少收集或补偿经人授权的培训数据的动力;
大规模部署此类管道的从业人员应当权衡这种取舍。

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
We have shown that the Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} – a
model-free, match-length measure of sequential complexity – is an effective
training-data filter against fine-tuning-driven model collapse: at
generation 6 it produces 42 % 42\% more unique trigrams, 30 % 30\% larger
vocabulary, and 19 % 19\% less intra-document repetition than unfiltered
training, while logprob-based filtering shows no significant diversity
benefit. For iterative pipelines where model internals are inaccessible, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering offers a strong, zero-cost baseline.

A natural concern is that the aggregate filtering advantage reported in
Table 1 could be driven by one domain in which H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} happens to be
a particularly good signal, while other domains show little or no benefit.

four domains – encyclopedic, scientific, conversational, and creative. The H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter advantage is present and directionally consistent across all four,

collapse manifests most severely as phrase-level repetition, the exact phenomenon H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} measures) and smallest in the creative domain. No domain shows the H L H_{L} -filter
outperforming unfiltered on H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , confirming that the null result for H L H_{L} -filtering is not an artefact of domain averaging.

blocks.en:
Section 5 argues that H L H_{L} -filtering fails because the within-generation H L H_{L} variance collapses after a single fine-tuning step, removing the ranking
signal the filter depends on. Figure 8 documents the starting
state that makes this explanation complete. At generation 0 – documents produced by
the base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model before any fine-tuning – the H L H_{L} distribution
is wide and bimodal (mean = 3.36 =3.36 , SD = 2.17 =2.17 ). The bimodality reflects
topic-dependent model familiarity: the base model assigns low entropy to topics
well-represented in its pretraining data and high entropy to unfamiliar topics,
producing two distinct modes rather than a smooth unimodal spread. After a single
generation of fine-tuning on 40 documents, the distribution collapses to a narrow
unimodal regime (SD ≈ 0.13 \approx 0.13 , a 17-fold reduction), where all topics are now
equally familiar to the fine-tuned model. From generation 1 onward, every document
receives a similar H L H_{L} score, so the H L H_{L} -filter’s ranking is determined by
noise rather than signal. The wide generation-0 distribution also explains why the H L H_{L} -filter is uncorrelated with H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} at generation 0 ( r = 0.18 r=0.18 , p = 0.11 p=0.11 ,
Section 3 ): the bimodal H L H_{L} variation captures topic familiarity,
not document diversity.
